content: Pain is a common symptom in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), but it is often underdiagnosed and inadequately treated. Recent clinical trials have explored various pharmacological treatments for managing pain associated with GBS. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of these treatments during both the acute phase and the convalescent phase (three months or more after onset) of GBS. A systematic search was conducted on November 3, 2014, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving participants with confirmed GBS, where pain assessment was either a primary or secondary outcome. Cross-over trials were included only if they had an adequate washout period between phases. Three short-term RCTs, involving a total of 277 participants in the acute phase of GBS, were included in the review. The risk of bias in these studies was generally unclear due to insufficient reporting. None of the studies reported the primary outcome of this review, which was the number of patients experiencing at least 50% self-reported pain relief. One small study compared a seven-day regimen of gabapentin to placebo in 18 participants. Pain was measured on a scale from 0 (no pain) to 10 (maximum pain). At the end of the study (day 7), participants in the gabapentin group had significantly lower mean pain scores compared to the placebo group (mean difference -3.61, 95% CI -4.12 to -3.10). However, the quality of this evidence was rated as very low. No significant differences were observed in the incidence of adverse events such as nausea (risk ratio [RR] 0.50, 95% CI 0.05 to 5.04) or constipation (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.54). A second study, involving 36 participants, compared gabapentin, carbamazepine, and placebo, all administered over seven days. Participants in the gabapentin group had significantly lower median pain scores on all treatment days compared to the placebo and carbamazepine groups (P < 0.05). While there were no significant differences in pain scores between the carbamazepine and placebo groups from day 1 to day 3, the carbamazepine group showed significantly lower median pain scores from day 4 to the end of the study (P < 0.05). The quality of this evidence was also rated as very low. Sedation was the only reported adverse effect of gabapentin and carbamazepine. A larger RCT, involving 223 participants who were all treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, compared a five-day course of methylprednisolone to placebo. This study found no statistically significant differences in the number of participants developing pain (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.16), the number of participants with decreased pain (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.42), or the number of participants with increased pain (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.41). The quality of this evidence was rated as low, and the study did not report whether there were any adverse events. In conclusion, this review found no new studies since its previous version. While pain management is a critical aspect of GBS treatment and pharmacological interventions are widely used, the current evidence does not provide strong support for the efficacy of any specific pharmacological treatment for GBS-associated pain. Although gabapentin and carbamazepine showed some reductions in pain severity compared to placebo, the evidence was limited and of very low quality. Larger, well-designed RCTs are needed to further evaluate the efficacy and safety of pharmacological treatments for pain in GBS. Additionally, future research should investigate interventions for managing pain during the convalescent phase of GBS.
